intro: Around 1388 Amersfoort built a second city wall, heaviest on the northeast side because that was the direction Gelre would come from. The wall is mostly gone and what is left of it is a park with old trees growing out of the rampart, including a catalpa that flowers hard enough to stop people. The oldest tree in the city is nowhere near it: an oak at a crossroads called the Hertekop, where a hunting lodge hung with antlers became a pub, then a meeting point, and then a motorway junction. The oak is what is left.
meta_description: 21 remarkable trees in Amersfoort: a catalpa on a 14th-century rampart, an oak that outlasted a motorway, and a plane the city built a school around.
question_meta: Amersfoort's oldest tree is the oak at the Hertekop crossroads, banded 1750 to 1800. Where it stands, and twenty more worth the walk.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Amersfoort is the oak at the Hertekop, on the Arnhemseweg where it crosses the Dodeweg beside the A28 slip road, which the national register places in a planting band of 1750 to 1800, so between about 225 and 275 years old. The crossroads takes its name from a hunting chalet that once stood there with deer antlers fixed to it. That building became an inn, then a well known meeting place and a starting point for walks and outings, and then it disappeared, when a southern ring road was laid around the city and later joined to a new trunk road from Utrecht. The junction that resulted bears no resemblance to the place the tree was planted in. The oak is the only part of the Hertekop still standing. One tree contests the title: a local tree expert dates the oak on the pond bank in Park Randenbroek to 1650, though the register bands it to the 1860s.
question_context: Ages here come from the Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen, which records a planting decade rather than a year, so every age on this page is a band and none is narrowed to look precise. The register is the 2024 edition and is the main source for these trees, which is why they are all flagged. One of them is a special case. The plane on the Schimmelpenninckkade grows inside the playground of the Sint Jorisschool, and an earlier version of this page left it out for that reason. It is here now because the register records it as both visitable and visible, and because you can see the whole crown from the public quay, which is where this page sends you: the yard is a working school and is not somewhere to walk into. Where the register describes a tree's condition we pass that on, as with the weeping lime in Park Schothorst, whose root flare is walked on constantly and which the register thinks is standing up to it. Pins marked approximate mean we know the place and not the trunk.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Amersfoort?
faq.a: The oak at the Hertekop crossroads on the Arnhemseweg, banded 1750 to 1800 by the national register. It is older than the ring road, the trunk road and the junction that now surround it, and older than the hunting lodge that gave the place its name.

faq.q: Why is there a park on the city wall?
faq.a: Because the wall came down and the earth bank did not. Amersfoort's second wall was built around 1388, concentrated on the northeast side against the threat from Gelre. What survives of it in the Plantsoen Oost was laid out as a park, so the old trees there are standing on a fourteenth century rampart.

faq.q: What is a weeping silver lime?
faq.a: A grafted cultivar. A weeping form is joined onto an ordinary lime rootstock, so on the tree in Park Schothorst you can find two different leaves: plain ones on shoots coming up from the stock below the graft, and above them the long-stalked leaves of the variety 'Petiolaris' hanging from arching branches.

All twenty-one can be seen from public ground, with two qualifications. The Plantsoen Oost, Park Schothorst and Park Randenbroek are public parks, the Hertekop oak stands at a road junction, and most of the rest are on streets, squares and a cemetery. The plane of the Sint Jorisschool is inside a school playground, so you look at it from the Schimmelpenninckkade rather than walking in.

trees.name: The Catalpa on the City Wall
trees.age_estimate: roughly 125 to 135 years, from the register's planting band of 1890 to 1900

location.address: Stadswal, Plantsoen Oost, behind Binnen de Veste 41

trees.story:
It is growing on a defensive earthwork built to keep the duke of Gelre out.

Around 1388 Amersfoort put up a second city wall, and put most of the effort into the northeast, because that was the side the trouble was expected from. The wall is largely gone. The bank it stood on is not, and the Plantsoen Oost is what the city made of the remains: a narrow park along the old rampart, planted with big trees whose roots are in six centuries of packed defensive earth.

The catalpa is behind Binnen de Veste 41 and the register singles it out for its flowering, which is fair. Catalpa flowers in late June and early July, weeks after everything else has finished, in upright panicles of white bells with yellow and purple markings inside the throat, and on a mature tree there are hundreds of them at once.

Then it produces the beans. Slender pods up to forty centimetres long hang all winter on the bare tree, which is where the name Indian bean tree comes from, and why this is worth a look in January as well.

Huge heart-shaped leaves, and it comes into leaf later than anything else in the park.
trees.access: Free. Public park on the old rampart, open at any time.
trees.transport: About 1 km east of Amersfoort station, on the eastern edge of the old centre.
trees.how_to_recognise: Very large heart-shaped leaves and long thin hanging pods. Bare when the rest of the park is green in May.

best_time.label: early July, when the whole crown is in white bells

trees.name: The Oak at the Hertekop
trees.age_estimate: roughly 225 to 275 years, from the register's planting band of 1750 to 1800

location.address: Beside the A28 slip road at the Arnhemseweg and Dodeweg crossing

trees.story:
Everything at this crossroads has been replaced except the tree.

It was called the Hertekop after a hunting chalet built here with deer antlers fixed to it. The chalet became an inn. The inn became one of those places everyone in a town knows, where people arranged to meet and where walks and outings started from. Then a southern ring road was laid around Amersfoort, and later joined to a new trunk road running in from Utrecht, and the place changed out of all recognition. The chalet went.

What is here now is a slip road off the A28 and a junction of the Arnhemseweg and the Dodeweg. What is also here is an oak the register bands 1750 to 1800, which was already a substantial tree when the chalet was a going concern, and which is the oldest living thing in Amersfoort.

It is not a beautiful setting and that is exactly the reason to go. Two and a half centuries of a place reorganising itself around a fixed point, and the fixed point is a tree that nobody decided to keep so much as never quite got round to removing.

Park on the Dodeweg rather than trying to stop on the Arnhemseweg.
trees.access: Free. Stands in the verge at a public road junction.
trees.transport: About 3 km south of Amersfoort station, at the Arnhemseweg and Dodeweg crossing.
trees.how_to_recognise: The single very heavy old oak at the junction, far thicker than the roadside planting around it.

best_time.label: October, when the acorns drop into the verge

trees.name: The Copper Beech of the Xaverius Church
trees.age_estimate: roughly 185 to 195 years, from the register's planting band of 1830 to 1840

location.address: By the St Franciscus Xavierius church, 't Zand 31

trees.story:
The church went up between 1881 and 1883. The beech was already about fifty years old when the first stone was laid.

That is worth pausing on, because the natural assumption at any church with a big tree beside it is that somebody planted the tree to go with the building. Here the register is explicit that the order runs the other way: banded 1830 to 1840, the beech predates the church by half a century, and whoever chose this plot chose a plot with a mature beech on it.

The register also gives it a health note, which is the sort of thing worth passing on. It calls the tree reasonably good for its age and for its position in an urban area, which is faint praise and honest. City copper beeches have a hard time of it: shallow feeding roots under paving, salt, and no leaf litter left to rot back into the soil.

Copper beech is not a species. It is a purple-leaved mutation of the common beech that turns up occasionally in the wild and is then propagated by grafting, so almost every one you meet was chosen by somebody.

In October the purple burns through to copper, and it is the best week to come.
trees.access: Free. Stands in the church grounds on 't Zand, reachable in daylight.
trees.transport: About 900 m east of Amersfoort station, on 't Zand.
trees.how_to_recognise: The large dark purple-leaved beech beside the church.

best_time.label: October, when the purple turns copper

trees.name: The Plane of the Snouckaertlaan
trees.age_estimate: roughly 185 to 195 years, from the register's planting band of 1830 to 1840

location.address: Snouckaertlaan 11, at the Utrechtseweg

trees.story:
A plane of this age on a Dutch street corner is a tree that has survived every plan anyone has had for the ground.

The register bands it 1830 to 1840, which puts it here before the villa quarter around it, before the Utrechtseweg was the road it is now, and before almost any of the buildings it stands among. It has spent nearly two centuries on the corner of the Snouckaertlaan while the city rearranged itself.

Planes get this job because they take punishment better than anything else their size. Compacted soil, roots cut for cables, salt, exhaust, and hard pruning: a plane shrugs at all of it and regrows. The species is a hybrid, probably of the oriental plane and the American sycamore, and it first appeared in European gardens in the seventeenth century as an accident of two exotic trees being planted near each other.

The bark is the giveaway and the reason it works in a city. It sheds in irregular plates, taking whatever has settled on it with it, so the trunk is a camouflage of cream, olive and grey that never blackens.

The seed balls hang on all winter, on stalks, like small hard fruit.
trees.access: Free. Street tree on public ground.
trees.transport: About 500 m southeast of Amersfoort station, at the top of the Snouckaertlaan.
trees.how_to_recognise: Flaking cream and olive bark, on the corner where the Snouckaertlaan meets the Utrechtseweg.

trees.name: The Weeping Silver Lime of Park Schothorst
trees.age_estimate: roughly 185 to 195 years, from the register's planting band of 1830 to 1840

location.address: Park Schothorst, at the back of the grounds on the edge of the wood

trees.story:
This tree carries two different kinds of leaf and you can find both from where you stand.

It is a grafted weeping lime. The weeping form, 'Petiolaris', cannot be grown from seed and is joined onto an ordinary lime rootstock, which means the tree is really two plants sharing a trunk. Above the graft the branches arch out and hang down, carrying leaves on unusually long stalks that let each one swing and show its white felted underside. Below the graft the rootstock keeps sending up its own shoots, and those carry plain lime leaves on short stalks. Look low on the trunk for ordinary foliage and up into the hanging branches for the long-stalked kind.

The register also notes the root flare, which is unusually pronounced and which people walk over constantly, and adds that the tree seems to be standing up to it. That is an honest way of saying it is being slowly damaged and is winning anyway.

It is at the back of Park Schothorst on the edge of the wood, banded 1830 to 1840.

Come in July. Silver limes flower late, and the scent of one this size carries a long way through a wood.
trees.access: Free. Public park, open daily.
trees.transport: About 3 km north of Amersfoort station, in Park Schothorst.
trees.how_to_recognise: Arching branches falling to the ground, leaves flashing white underneath, and a heavy exposed root flare at the base.

best_time.label: July, when it flowers late and the scent carries through the wood

trees.name: The Copper Beech behind the Amershof
trees.age_estimate: roughly 135 to 145 years, from the register's planting band of 1880 to 1890

location.address: By the back entrance of the Amershof, Burgemeester De Widtstraat

trees.story:
It is at the back entrance of a function venue, which is a demotion, and it is the reason to look.

A copper beech planted between 1880 and 1890 was put in by somebody laying out a garden. Nobody plants a purple beech at a service door. So this tree has been through the usual sequence for a city centre: a private garden, a change of ownership, a building extended over most of the ground, and the tree left standing in the leftover space that the extension did not need, which happened to be by the back door.

It is a common story and it accounts for a striking share of the big old trees in any Dutch city centre. The ones that survive are rarely the ones that were treasured. They are the ones that were standing somewhere nobody wanted to build.

What you get is a full grown copper beech in a small hard space on the Burgemeester De Widtstraat, dark and dense and considerably too large for its surroundings, which is a good look at what the species does when nothing restrains it but paving.

Best in October and, for a different reason, in April, when the new leaves come out a translucent red before they darken.
trees.access: Free. Visible and reachable from the street at the back of the building.
trees.transport: About 700 m east of Amersfoort station, on the Burgemeester De Widtstraat.
trees.how_to_recognise: A large purple beech crowded into the paved space by the venue's rear entrance.

best_time.label: April, when the new leaves open translucent red

trees.name: The Copper Beech at the Zonnehof
trees.age_estimate: roughly 135 to 145 years, from the register's planting band of 1880 to 1890

location.address: Northeast side of Zonnehof 2, behind the building on the Utrechtseweg

trees.story:
The Zonnehof is a piece of open ground on the edge of the old centre that the twentieth century got hold of, and this beech was standing before any of it.

Banded 1880 to 1890, it belongs to the villa gardens that lined the Utrechtseweg when this was the smart approach to the city rather than a through road. Those gardens have gone. The beech is on the northeast side of Zonnehof 2, behind the building that fronts the Utrechtseweg, which is to say in the gap between two eras of construction.

Standing under a copper beech in a city is a specific experience worth going out of your way for. The leaves are thin and the purple pigment is a filter rather than a coating, so strong light coming through a mature canopy arrives underneath as a deep wine red. Photographs never get it because a camera corrects it away. You have to be under it, and it wants a bright day.

This one is a short walk from the plane on the Snouckaertlaan and from the beech behind the Amershof, so all three fit into twenty minutes.

The fourth week of October, if you want it at full colour.
trees.access: Free. Reachable on foot from the Zonnehof, open at any time.
trees.transport: About 500 m southeast of Amersfoort station, at the Zonnehof.
trees.how_to_recognise: On the northeast side of the building at Zonnehof 2, a full-sized purple beech in an open paved setting.

trees.name: The Plane of the Sint Jorisschool
trees.age_estimate: roughly 175 to 185 years, from the register's planting band of 1840 to 1850

location.address: Schoolyard of the Sint Jorisschool, Schimmelpenninckkade, Amersfoort

trees.story:
When the Sint Jorisschool went up in 1910 this plane was already seventy years old, and the builders left it where it was. It has stood in a schoolyard ever since.

It was planted between 1840 and 1850, when the site was still a green strip along the quay of the river Eem. The strip was built over in 1910 and the new school opened with four classes on the quay side, with a full grown tree already in front of it. That building came down in 1992 and its replacement went up straight away. The register notes, drily, that the tree was reasonably well protected during the works.

It is close to two hundred years old now, six metres round at chest height and 27.8 metres tall, with a crown twenty-seven metres across, which is wider than the yard it stands in.

Benches used to ring the base for the pupils. At the end of 2021 the paving came out and the yard was resurfaced in wood chips, some of the benches were taken away, and the children moved onto the roots instead. After everything else this tree has absorbed, the register's verdict is that it seems to cope well.

You can see the whole crown from the quay.
trees.access: Free to look at. The tree stands on the Sint Jorisschool playground and the whole crown is in view from the Schimmelpenninckkade, which is a public quay. The register lists it as visitable, but it is a working schoolyard, so stand on the quay rather than walking in.
trees.transport: About 15 minutes on foot from Amersfoort Centraal, on the Schimmelpenninckkade beside the Eem.

photo.attribution: WeeJeeVee, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.how_to_recognise: One enormous plane rising alone out of a walled schoolyard set below the level of the quay, its crown far wider than the yard, flaking cream and olive bark on a single straight trunk.

trees.name: The Plane of the Catholic Cemetery
trees.age_estimate: roughly 126 to 136 years, from the register's planting band of 1890 to 1900

location.address: RK begraafplaats, Utrechtseweg, south-west section, Amersfoort

trees.story:
This plane stands in the south-west corner of Amersfoort's Catholic cemetery on the Utrechtseweg, tall enough now to be visible over the cemetery wall from the street outside.

London planes were planted in Dutch cemeteries through the late nineteenth century for a practical reason: the species tolerates compacted soil and heavy shade better than almost anything else that grows this large, which matters on ground crossed with paths and graves. The bark comes away in patches the size of a hand as the trunk outgrows its own skin, leaving a mottled grey, green and cream pattern that is the tree's normal healthy state rather than any kind of damage.

The register bands its planting to the 1890s, putting it just past its first century and a quarter. Cemetery trees like this one are some of the least disturbed in any Dutch town, since nobody prunes a graveyard tree for looking untidy the way a street tree gets cut back.

Free to visit. The cemetery is open during daylight hours, as is normal for a working Catholic burial ground, and a walk between the graves brings you directly under the crown.
trees.access: Free. Cemetery grounds, open during daylight hours.
trees.transport: About 625 m south of Amersfoort station, on the Utrechtseweg.
trees.how_to_recognise: The plane in the cemetery's south-west section, tall enough to show over the boundary wall from the Utrechtseweg.

trees.name: The Copper Beech of the Old Library
trees.age_estimate: roughly 156 to 166 years, from the register's planting band of 1860 to 1870

location.address: East side next to Zonnehof 12, former library, Amersfoort

trees.story:
This copper beech stands where Amersfoort's old public library used to be, on the east side of the Zonnehof, and it has outlasted the building it once stood beside.

Copper beech is not a separate species but a colour form of the ordinary European beech, its leaves carrying a red pigment on top of the usual green, which is why the whole crown reads dark purple-bronze rather than green from any distance. Amersfoort already has more than one of these registered within the town centre, and this is among the oldest.

The register bands its planting to the 1860s, close to a century and three quarters old, which makes it a decade or two senior to the copper beeches at the Amershof and the Zonnehof building nearby.

Free, public green strip in the centre of town, no gate.

October is the month, when the copper deepens toward black just before the leaves drop.
trees.access: Free. Reachable on foot from the Zonnehof, open at any time.
trees.transport: About 766 m south-east of Amersfoort station, near the Zonnehof.
trees.how_to_recognise: The oldest of Amersfoort's several copper beeches, standing on the site of the former public library.

best_time.label: October, when the copper deepens toward black before the leaves drop

trees.name: The Sweet Chestnut of the Old Barracks
trees.age_estimate: roughly 116 to 126 years, from the register's planting band of 1900 to 1910

location.address: Juliana van Stolberg park, Leusderweg side, on former barracks ground, Amersfoort

trees.story:
This sweet chestnut grows on what the register itself calls former barracks ground, on the Leusderweg side of what is now Juliana van Stolberg park.

Castanea sativa produces the only true edible chestnut among Amersfoort's monumental trees, distinct from the inedible conkers of the horse chestnuts elsewhere on this page. Its leaves are long, narrow and sharply toothed along the edge, easy to tell apart from any other tree in a Dutch park at a glance, and in October the spiny husks split open on the ground to drop chestnuts a forager can actually use.

The register bands its planting to 1900 to 1910, so it went into the ground while this was still working military land rather than the public green space it later became. A chestnut planted on a barracks ground for shade has quietly outlived the barracks by a century.

Free, public park, open daily.

October is the month, when the husks come down. Gather what falls rather than what is still on the tree, and expect competition from the local squirrels.
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily.
trees.transport: About 906 m south of Amersfoort station, in Juliana van Stolberg park.
trees.how_to_recognise: The long, sharply toothed leaves mark it as a sweet chestnut rather than a horse chestnut; it stands on the Leusderweg side of the park.

best_time.label: October, when the spiny husks split and drop real, edible chestnuts

trees.name: The Hungarian Oak of Randenbroek
trees.age_estimate: roughly 156 to 166 years, from the register's planting band of 1860 to 1870

location.address: Rubensstraat, former car park, now a green strip, Randenbroek, Amersfoort

trees.story:
Most oaks in a Dutch park are the native pedunculate oak. This one is not: it is a Hungarian oak, native to the Balkans and south-eastern Europe, and its leaves give it away immediately, glossier and more deeply cut than any local oak, with lobes that reach almost to the midrib.

Quercus frainetto was brought into northern European planting for a practical reason: it tolerates poorer, drier soils than the native oak and still grows into a broad, substantial crown. This one stands on what used to be a car park in the Randenbroek neighbourhood, now a green strip on the Rubensstraat, which says something about how a tree this size can outlast several changes of use for the ground beneath it.

The register bands its planting to the 1860s, making it roughly a century and a half old and one of the more unusual species on Amersfoort's register within the town itself.

Free, public green strip, no gate, open at all times.

There is no single spectacular month. The reason to find this one is simply that it is not the oak you already know, standing in an ordinary residential street rather than a grand park.
trees.access: Free. Public green strip, no gate.
trees.transport: About 1.3 km south-east of Amersfoort station, in Randenbroek.
trees.how_to_recognise: Glossier, more deeply lobed leaves than any native oak nearby; stands on a former car park turned green strip on the Rubensstraat.

best_time.label: late October, when the oak on the Rubensstraat strip turns russet and yellow

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of the Station Square
trees.age_estimate: roughly 96 to 106 years, from the register's planting band of 1920 to 1930

location.address: Stationsplein, Amersfoort

trees.story:
Amersfoort's registered horse chestnut stands on the station square itself, which means more people probably walk past this tree on an ordinary Tuesday than pass any other tree on this page in a month.

Aesculus hippocastanum is the classic candle-flowered chestnut of European squares and avenues, and this one has done its job in one of the more heavily used public spaces in the city since the 1920s, when the register bands its planting. It has had a harder run than a park tree of the same age: the horse chestnut leaf miner moth, in the Netherlands since around 2002, browns the foliage of nearly every chestnut in the country by late summer, and bleeding canker has killed mature specimens across the region since the 1990s. A century-old chestnut still standing on a station square, with commuters and buses passing under it daily, is a tree that has held up.

Free to see, no ticket, right outside Amersfoort's main railway station.

Come in the first half of May for the white candle-shaped flower spikes, before the leaf miner starts its usual damage later in the summer.
trees.access: Free. Public square, no ticket.
trees.transport: About 100 m from Amersfoort Centraal, on the Stationsplein.
trees.how_to_recognise: The single registered chestnut standing on the station square itself, outside Amersfoort Centraal.

best_time.label: early May, before the leaf miner moths brown the leaves

trees.name: The Red Horse Chestnut by the Tower
trees.age_estimate: roughly 136 to 146 years, from the register's planting band of 1880 to 1890

location.address: Between the Onze Lieve Vrouwetoren and the Varkensmarkt, Amersfoort

trees.story:
This red-flowered chestnut stands between the Onze Lieve Vrouwetoren, Amersfoort's freestanding medieval tower, and the old Varkensmarkt square, which makes it one of the more photographed backdrops in the city without anyone particularly meaning to photograph the tree itself.

Aesculus x carnea is a hybrid between the familiar white-flowered horse chestnut and a smaller red-flowered American species, and the cross keeps the size of the European parent while borrowing the American parent's pink to red flower colour, which is what sets it apart from the plain horse chestnut on the station square nearby.

The register bands its planting to the 1880s, putting it well past its first century, growing in the shadow of a tower that has stood since the fifteenth century and makes even a tree this old look young by comparison.

Free, public street, no gate.

May is the month for the pink candles, timed a week or two alongside the white-flowered horse chestnut by the station, so a short walk between the two shows both colours at once.
trees.access: Free. Public street, no gate.
trees.transport: About 850 m east of Amersfoort station, between the tower and the Varkensmarkt.
trees.how_to_recognise: Pink to red flower candles rather than white, standing between the medieval tower and the Varkensmarkt.

best_time.label: May, when the candles come out pink rather than the usual white

trees.name: The Bald Cypress at the Monnikendam
trees.age_estimate: roughly 190 years

location.address: Zuidsingel 36, Amersfoort

trees.access: Free to view from the Zuidsingel street and the Monnikendam bridge. The tree stands inside a private garden behind the gate and is not open to enter: the register lists it as visible but not visitable.
trees.transport: About 400 m east of Amersfoort station, beside the historic Monnikendam water gate on the Zuidsingel/Kortegracht.
trees.story:
The oldest tree in this garden is no longer in it. A copper beech planted in 1750, counted among the twenty oldest trees in the country by the Bomenstichting, stood behind the Monnikendam until it was felled. The cypress on the far side of the water is still there, and three separate sources agree on when it went in: 1830.

That agreement is worth noting, because it almost never happens. The national tree register, a Wageningen-linked city nature walk and the municipality's own tree-walk booklet all place a Taxodium distichum in this private garden and all give the same planting year, which puts the tree at roughly 190 years.

It is a conifer that behaves like a broadleaf. In its home range, the swamp forests of the American southeast, it stands in standing water and pushes woody knees up through the mud; here it turns rust red in November, drops every needle, and spends the winter looking dead before leafing out again in late spring.

Behind it is the Monnikendam itself, the water gate of Amersfoort's second city wall, built around 1400 and now holding a restaurant. The garden is private and you cannot walk in. You look at the tree from the Zuidsingel or from the bridge, which is exactly how the nature walk describes it: on the left of the water, an old cypress.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the conifer that stands bare through the winter and leafs out late, rusty red in November. It is in the private garden on the far side of the water, seen from the Zuidsingel or the Monnikendam bridge.

best_time.label: November, when the needles turn foxy red and then drop

trees.name: The King's Lime at the Stadsring
trees.age_estimate: roughly 90 years

location.address: Corner of Stadsring and Molenstraat, Amersfoort

trees.access: Free. Stands on a raised stone plateau on a public street corner, no gate.
trees.transport: About 230 m northwest of Amersfoort station, at the corner of Stadsring and Molenstraat.
trees.story:
Two official sources agree that this lime was planted for the House of Orange and disagree about which occasion. The national tree register lists it as the Juliana-Bernhard wedding tree, for the marriage of Princess Juliana and Prince Bernhard in January 1937. The municipality's own tree-walk booklet, describing the same tree on the same raised stone plateau on this corner, says it went in during 1938 for the birth of Princess Beatrix. Both years fall inside the register's 1930 to 1940 planting band, the two occasions are a year apart, and nothing we found settles which one this tree marks.

The confusion is almost the tree's own fault. It is a Koningslinde, a selection of common lime bred in the Netherlands specifically to be planted at royal occasions, the tree a town council orders when a wedding, a coronation or a birth needs marking in wood. Amersfoort had two of those within thirteen months and put a lime on a plateau at the corner of the Stadsring and Molenstraat.

Whichever event it commemorates, it was in the ground before the occupation and it is still there. Beatrix was born, became queen, reigned for thirty-three years and abdicated in 2013, and the lime has kept its plateau on one of the busiest corners in town throughout.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by where it stands: alone on a raised stone plateau right on the corner of the Stadsring and Molenstraat, a single lime set above the pavement rather than planted in it.

best_time.label: June to July, when it flowers

trees.name: The Last Lime of the Westsingel
trees.age_estimate: roughly 250 years

location.address: Westsingel 50, by the entrance to Museum Flehite, Amersfoort

trees.access: Free. Public street/park ground beside the bridge to Museum Flehite, open at any time.
trees.transport: About 420 m north of Amersfoort station, on the Westsingel next to the bridge to Museum Flehite.
trees.story:
This lime is hollow, rotted through the middle, and the last one standing of its row. It still comes into full leaf every spring.

The register entry originally covered a whole line of common limes along the Westsingel, planted somewhere between 1750 and 1800. One is left. The municipality's own tree-walk booklet puts a Hollandse linde at this exact spot by the bridge to Museum Flehite and dates it to 1800, the young end of the register's band, so the honest figure is somewhere between 225 and 275 years rather than a single year anyone can point to. Young limes have since been replanted alongside it, which makes the comparison easy: they are the same species and a fraction of the girth.

The hollowness is not the emergency it sounds like. A lime lives in its outer wood, and the heart can rot away entirely while the tree goes on putting out leaves; pollarding, which is the form the register records for this one, tends to extend that career rather than shorten it.

It stands in front of a museum whose collection includes a painted view of Amersfoort from 1671, made about a century before anybody pushed this lime into the ground. This tree is the last of the avenue that once lined the singel, and it is doing the job of all of them.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, hollow and pollarded and far thicker than the young limes replanted beside it. It stands right at the bridge to Museum Flehite on the Westsingel.

best_time.label: January and February, when the leaves are off and the hollow pollarded trunk is the whole story

trees.name: The Lime of the Havik
trees.age_estimate: roughly 140 years by the register; about 175 years by a local tree expert's estimate

location.address: Havik, next to the Bolle brug, Amersfoort

trees.access: Free. Public canal-side street in the old town, no gate.
trees.transport: About 400 m north of Amersfoort station, on the Havik beside the Bolle brug.
trees.story:
Every other old lime along this quay was cut back hard and made to grow again. This one was left alone, and it is the tree that still gives the Havik its shape. The national register's own history for the Havik-linde says the two rows that once lined both sides of the water were all rejuvenated at some point, except this one, and that it is in good health.

The water it stands on was a working harbour. Havik comes from Havenwijk, the harbour quarter, and this short canal was where medieval Amersfoort loaded and unloaded before the trade moved on and the quay became a street of houses with a bridge in the middle of it.

The age is where the sources part company. The Bomenstichting register puts the planting between 1880 and 1890 and places the tree beside the Bolle brug. An older city nature walk dates the surviving Havik lime to 1850, and a local tree expert's list, sent to us through IVN Amersfoort in October 2026, also gives 1850 for the lime beside the bridge. So the page carries both: about 140 years by the register, about 175 by local reckoning.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the one full-grown lime on the quay: the others along the Havik were cut back and regrown, so they read as visibly younger. It stands on the canal side of the street beside the Bolle brug.

best_time.label: June to July, when it flowers

trees.name: The Oak at the Randenbroek Pond
trees.age_estimate: about 160 years by the register; about 375 years by a local tree expert's estimate

location.address: Behind the house on the bank of the pond, Park Randenbroek, Heiligenbergerweg, Amersfoort

trees.access: Free. Public municipal park around the house of Randenbroek, no ticket.
trees.transport: About 2 km on foot south-east of Amersfoort Centraal, and about 700 m south of the Monnikendam water gate.
trees.story:
Two counts put this oak two centuries apart. The national register of monumental trees bands its planting to the 1860s, which makes it about 160 years old. A local tree expert's list, sent to us through IVN Amersfoort in October 2026, names it as the oldest tree in the city and dates it to 1650, which would make it about 375. This page carries both.

If the local date is right, the oak went into the ground while the painter and architect Jacob van Campen, who designed Amsterdam's town hall, was living here. He was granted Randenbroek in 1626, made the house habitable again after imperial troops occupying Amersfoort burned it in 1629, and turned a farm on marshy ground into a pleasure garden with fish ponds, fountains, orchards and a vineyard of more than forty kinds of grape. When the estate was sold in 1739, the notice listed its plantings of oak, elm and beech.

After 1814 the formal garden was remade in the landscape style, with new paths and ponds, and trees were felled to make room for them. This one stands behind the house on the bank of the pond, 5.34 metres round and 25 metres tall by the register's measure. In 2002 the register noted that its dead tops had been cut out, leaving a crown shaped more or less like a candelabra.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 5.34 metres round and 25 metres tall. It stands behind the house of Randenbroek, on the bank of the pond.
trees.verify_notes: 2026-10-19: LRMB 1677723 (status 3 monumental, last observed 2024-07-17), Zomereik, planted 1860-1870, girth 534 cm, height 25 m, municipal, visitable; 2002 remark: dead tops removed, crown now more or less candelabra-shaped. IVN Amersfoort forwarded a local tree expert's list (October 2026) naming this oak 'Park Randenbroek op terras aan de grote vijver', planted 1650, as the oldest; both ages published, not chosen between. Estate history from the Rijksmonumentenregister complex 529188. The expert's name is not recorded here.

trees.name: The Planes at the Randenbroek Gate
trees.age_estimate: about 160 years (register planting band 1860 to 1870)

location.address: Main entrance of Park Randenbroek, Amersfoort

trees.access: Free. Public municipal park around the house of Randenbroek, no ticket.
trees.transport: About 2 km on foot south-east of Amersfoort Centraal; the oak by the pond is about 250 m into the park.
trees.story:
The house at Randenbroek has been rebuilt, extended, cut back and restored since these two planes went in, and they are still at the gate. The national register of monumental trees lists them as a pair at the main entrance to the park, bands their planting to the 1860s and records a trunk 4.81 metres round and a height of 30 metres.

In the 1860s Randenbroek was a private country house that changed hands often. It had been auctioned in 1833, shortly after the house was renewed in the fashion of the day, and in 1873 Godert Jan Adolph van Hardenbroek laid the first stone of an extension on the brook side of the house. The planes have outlasted that wing: it was taken down again in the restoration of 1958.

The estate is now a public park owned by the city, and the register's most recent look at the pair was in the summer of 2026, so these are about 160 years old and still standing guard. Nobody has written down who planted them or which owner wanted them there. If you know, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the pair of planes at the main entrance of Park Randenbroek, about 30 metres tall, one trunk 4.81 metres round.
trees.verify_notes: 2026-10-19: LRMB 1680326 (status 3 monumental, last observed 2026-07-03), Gewone plataan, 2 trees (municipal numbers 56904 and 56905), planted 1860-1870, girth 481 cm, height 30 m, municipal, visitable; register place note 'Op kaart locatie verbeterd' (map location corrected). Single register source, flagged; the July 2026 observation is the life check. Estate history from the Rijksmonumentenregister complex 529188.

trees.name: The Yew of Randenbroek
trees.age_estimate: about 160 years (register planting band 1860 to 1870)

location.address: Near the main house, Park Randenbroek, Amersfoort

trees.access: Free. Public municipal park around the house of Randenbroek, no ticket.
trees.transport: About 2 km on foot south-east of Amersfoort Centraal, a few steps from the house and the oak by the pond.
trees.story:
Most yews stop well short of twenty metres. This one, near the house at Randenbroek, has reached nineteen, and it has done it on two stems. The national register of monumental trees measures it at 3.34 metres round and bands its planting to the 1860s, which makes it about 160 years old.

By the standards of its species that is young. Yews are the long-lived trees of European churchyards and gardens, and a yew of 160 is only getting started. The reason to come and look is its height and its shape, not its age.

Yew is everywhere else in this park, kept low. The city's management plan for Randenbroek counts about 700 metres of yew hedge, clipped to 80 centimetres, around the old kitchen garden and the house, and keeps yew, holly and rhododendron as the undergrowth of the wooded part of the park. This is the one that was allowed to grow into a tree.

The estate it stands on goes back to a farm on marshy ground, owned by the bishops of Utrecht in the fourteenth century and turned into a country house with gardens by the architect Jacob van Campen after 1626. The landscape park around it dates from the years after 1814.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its two stems and its height, 19 metres, tall for a yew. It stands near the house of Randenbroek.

Yew hedges (700 m at 80 cm) and yew undergrowth from the city's Beheerplan Park Randenbroek. Single register source, flagged.
